particulars: All names, dates, locations, store names, dollar amounts, sentence lengths, physical measurements, print point counts, statute and agency names, and the year-by-year timeline are absent from the reading.

items.record: The harm was two armed robberies of retail stores by a stranger: "a man with a gun robbed a Family Dollar store" and a Dollar Tree was "robbed at gunpoint of $208."
items.reading: The harm happened "inside a household, not between strangers"; the victims are probably a child, partner or elderly parent.
items.loss: This misidentifies the basic offence and the relationship between offender and victims.

items.record: The man convicted was apparently not the robber. The case ends with the conviction undone: "granted the motion for a new trial, and the state dismissed the charge."
items.reading: The judgment "produces a durable official truth"; the record "stands", with a possible appeal pending.
items.loss: This misses the overall arc of a wrongful conviction that was eventually reversed and dismissed.

items.record: The accused consistently denied guilt and offered his own life as the reason: "he worked full-time at a local factory, owned a $40,000 car and had no need to rob dollar stores"; "It wasn't me, your honor."
items.reading: The defendant "explained the harm away as discipline, accident, stress", and the court dismantles that rationalization.
items.loss: This misdescribes the defendant's stance as excusing harm when it was a flat claim of innocence.

items.record: The conviction rested on shaky eyewitness picks. Witnesses chose no one at first and picked him only on a second look, with partial certainty: "selected Brown, writing: 'I think it was him... 80 percent.'"
items.reading: Witnesses are family members who "may have given evidence against people they love."
items.loss: This misses the evidentiary mechanism of uncertain, repeated stranger identifications.

items.record: The identifications were cross-racial and did not match the accused's build. The witness noted he looked "'lighter' and 'smaller' and 'skinny' compared with the robber", and medical records showed "5 feet 9 inches and 150 pounds" against descriptions of 6 feet and 200 or more pounds.
items.loss: This omits the physical mismatch between the description and the accused that should have undercut the identification.

items.record: Police used a suggestive procedure on one witness: "an officer pointed to Brown's photo and asked whether she was sure it wasn't him."
items.loss: This omits police conduct that steered witnesses toward the suspect.

items.record: A witness who knew him as a regular customer testified for the defence that he was not the robber, and the prosecution confronted her with an earlier statement: "'I know it's not him.'"
items.reading: Witnesses share loyalties with the defendant and testify against him.
items.loss: This misses the split among witnesses and the prosecution's effort to discredit the exculpatory one.

items.record: The fingerprint examiner's work was faulty and misreported. His report said he had searched the state database, but the prints were "loaded but never searched"; he called the gum print of no value when it "did have value and appeared to be a whorl, a pattern Brown does not have."
items.loss: This omits the forensic failure and the false report at the centre of the conviction.

items.record: The examiner testified that no usable print survives cleaning with Windex, but "research published as early as 2012 showed latent prints routinely survive commercial cleaning products."
items.loss: This omits how inaccurate expert testimony explained away the absence of other prints.

items.record: When the database search was finally run, it pointed to another man: "one of the three prints came from a man identified as Daris J.... who was taller and heavier than Brown."
items.loss: This omits the discovery of an alternative suspect that broke the case open.

items.record: The jury was divided and pushed toward agreement, then returned a split verdict: "Judge Henry Hight gave an Allen charge urging a unanimous verdict"; the jury acquitted on one robbery and convicted on the other.
items.loss: This omits the jury dynamics and the inconsistent verdict on two robberies attributed to the same man.

items.record: Trial counsel failed to present available evidence: he did not show that Brown "did not fit the witness descriptions or resemble the man on the surveillance video", did not seek an eyewitness-reform instruction, and used no independent print expert.
items.reading: "Vigorous mitigation that the court engages with directly."
items.loss: This misses inadequate defence at trial as a cause of the conviction.

items.record: Evidence was destroyed after conviction and the claim failed on a high bar: "no due-process violation because there was no proof the clerk had acted in bad faith."
items.loss: This omits loss of evidence by the institution and the legal standard that left the defendant without a remedy.

items.record: Post-conviction relief came only after years of defence digging against institutional non-cooperation: "The police department said it had no records... and did not answer the SAFIS question"; the court ordered the review of the examiner disclosed.
items.reading: The "counter-force" is most plausibly a single appeal or sentencing challenge.
items.loss: This misses the long, staged process by which an innocence organisation forced disclosure from reluctant agencies.

items.record: Early challenges failed: the conviction was affirmed on appeal and the destruction claim was rejected, and he was "released from prison" before he was cleared.
items.loss: This omits the sequence of failed remedies and the fact that the sentence was served before vindication.

items.record: The state consented to a new trial while defending the system: it cited a "'reasonable probability that someone else... was in fact the individual'" while "maintaining that Brown's trial lawyer had been effective."
items.reading: The court authoritatively finds against the defendant.
items.loss: This misses that the prosecution itself conceded the case while protecting the institution's record.

items.record: The "family" element in the record is the defendant's own life, offered as evidence of innocence: "I had a full-time job and custody of my son"; he was seen "often with a little boy."
items.reading: The family is the site of the harm, and the defendant is an abusive relative.
items.loss: This inverts the role of family, from the source of the crime to the defendant's character and alibi context.

items.record: The apparent strength of the case was the illusion. A print "match" and eyewitness picks looked solid but later dissolved: the print attributed to Brown was later rated "'medium-low' quality."
items.reading: The illusion is either the court's neat narrative of a family or the defendant's rationalized story.
items.loss: This misidentifies what was illusory: the seemingly strong forensic and eyewitness evidence of guilt.

items.record: The text is a chronological case history of an exoneration spanning a dozen years, with many proceedings, not a single document.
items.reading: A single court judgment or sentencing decision stating findings and issuing directions.
items.loss: This misidentifies the form and time span of the record.
